title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 15
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Symbiosis: Mutualism in Nature
passages.text:
Symbiosis refers to a close, long-term relationship between individuals of different species, and encompasses a spectrum of associations ranging from parasitism, in which one organism benefits at the expense of another, to mutualism, in which both organisms derive benefits from their interaction. Mutualistic relationships are among the most ecologically important and widespread associations in nature, operating across virtually every ecosystem and at multiple scales of biological organisation, from subcellular symbioses within eukaryotic cells to ecosystem-level interactions between predators and their prey.

One of the most striking examples of mutualism occurs between flowering plants and their animal pollinators. Flowering plants have evolved elaborate floral structures, colours, fragrances, and nectar rewards that attract insects, birds, or bats. These pollinators visit flowers to feed on nectar, and in doing so, inadvertently transfer pollen from flower to flower, enabling plant reproduction. Both parties benefit: plants achieve reproduction without expending the metabolic cost of producing sufficient pollen to rely on random wind dispersal, while pollinators gain a reliable food source. This mutualistic relationship has driven the diversification of both flowering plants and their pollinator fauna, shaping the structure of terrestrial ecosystems over the past 100 million years.

Another fundamental mutualistic system involves the relationship between plants and mycorrhizal fungi. Mycorrhizal fungi form networks of threadlike structures called hyphae that extend through soil and penetrate plant roots. The fungus provides the plant with access to water and mineral nutrients, particularly phosphorus and nitrogen, that might otherwise be inaccessible due to the limited reach of root systems. In exchange, the plant provides the fungus with photosynthetically derived sugars, which the fungus cannot produce independently. This relationship is so ancient and pervasive that the majority of terrestrial plant species depend on mycorrhizal associations for optimal nutrient acquisition.

Mutualistic relationships extend into the animal kingdom as well. Cleaner fish remove parasites and dead skin from the bodies of larger fish, gaining food while their clients benefit from improved health and reduced infection risk. Similarly, oxpeckers — birds that inhabit African savannas — feed on parasitic insects and dead skin from mammals such as zebras and rhinoceroses. Some mutualistic relationships are obligate, meaning one or both organisms cannot survive without their partner; others are facultative, allowing organisms to survive independently if necessary. The evolution of mutualism often involves the development of specialised signalling mechanisms and behavioural adaptations that enable reliable partner recognition and prevent exploitation by cheaters.

Mutualistic relationships are fundamental to ecosystem functioning and provide essential ecosystem services that humanity depends upon. Pollination services alone are valued at hundreds of billions of dollars annually, supporting agricultural production worldwide. Mycorrhizal associations enable nutrient cycling critical to soil health and forest productivity. The disruption of mutualistic relationships through habitat loss, pollution, or climate change therefore has cascading consequences for ecosystem stability. Understanding mutualism is essential for addressing contemporary environmental challenges and developing sustainable practices that maintain the services ecosystems provide.

passages.title: The Neuroscience of Language
passages.text:
Language represents one of the most complex and distinctive cognitive capacities of the human brain, enabling abstract thought, cultural transmission, and complex social coordination. Over the past several decades, neuroscience research has progressively elucidated the neural mechanisms underlying language production, comprehension, and learning, revealing that language involves intricate networks spanning multiple brain regions rather than being localised in any single area.

The traditional view, formulated in the nineteenth century, identified two primary language centres: Broca's area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus of the left hemisphere, and Wernicke's area, situated in the superior temporal gyrus of the left hemisphere. Broca's area was associated with language production, while Wernicke's area was associated with language comprehension. However, contemporary neuroimaging studies reveal that this model is oversimplified. Damage to Broca's area does not eliminate speech production entirely, and conversely, damage to Wernicke's area does not completely abolish comprehension. Modern neuroscience recognises that language involves distributed networks encompassing not only traditional language areas but also frontal regions associated with syntax processing, temporal regions involved in semantic meaning, and parietal regions that integrate multimodal information.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) have enabled researchers to map patterns of neural activation during language tasks in healthy, intact brains. These studies demonstrate that listening to language, reading text, and producing speech recruit overlapping but distinct neural systems. Comprehension involves networks that process phonological information (the sounds of language), syntactic structure (the grammatical rules), and semantic meaning (the conceptual content). Each of these components engages different neural regions, suggesting a modular organisation of language processing in the brain.

Language learning is supported by neural plasticity — the brain's capacity to reorganise and form new connections in response to experience. Children acquiring their native language show rapid strengthening of neural pathways supporting phonological distinctions specific to their language. Adults learning a second language recruit slightly different neural networks than native speakers, engaging regions associated with deliberate, effortful processing; however, with extensive practice and immersion, second-language learners gradually shift toward the same neural substrates used by native speakers. This neural reorganisation reflects behavioural improvement, as adult learners progressively achieve native-like proficiency.

Language disorders such as aphasia, dyslexia, and specific language impairment represent disruptions to the neural systems underlying language. Aphasia, typically resulting from stroke or brain injury affecting language areas, manifests in various forms depending on which regions are damaged. Broca's aphasia, for instance, results in agrammatic speech with preserved comprehension, while Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension. Understanding the neural basis of language disorders has enabled development of targeted rehabilitation strategies. Neuroplasticity research suggests that intensive training can partially recover lost language functions by strengthening alternative neural pathways, offering hope for language recovery following brain injury.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is the key difference between parasitism and mutualism?
questions.correctAnswer: In parasitism one organism benefits at the expense of another; in mutualism both organisms benefit
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 defines parasitism as 'one organism benefits at the expense of another' and mutualism as 'both organisms derive benefits.'
options: In parasitism one organism benefits at the expense of another; in mutualism both organisms benefit
They are the same phenomenon with different names
Parasitism involves more species than mutualism
Both are temporary relationships

questions.prompt: The word 'elaborate' in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: complex and intricate in design
questions.explanation: 'Elaborate floral structures' refers to complex, ornate, carefully developed structures.
options: purely functional
complex and intricate in design
simple and straightforward
temporary and fragile

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, how do flowering plants benefit from their mutualistic relationship with pollinators?
questions.correctAnswer: They achieve reproduction without producing excessive pollen through wind dispersal
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states plants 'achieve reproduction without expending the metabolic cost of producing sufficient pollen to rely on random wind dispersal.'
options: They gain access to water and minerals
They are protected from predators
They achieve reproduction without producing excessive pollen through wind dispersal
They obtain photosynthetic energy

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the evolutionary age of the plant-mycorrhizal fungus relationship?
questions.correctAnswer: It is extremely ancient, having evolved over hundreds of millions of years
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes this relationship as 'so ancient and pervasive' that 'the majority of terrestrial plant species depend on it.'
options: It has existed for only about 100,000 years
The evolutionary timeline is unknown
It evolved recently in geological time
It is extremely ancient, having evolved over hundreds of millions of years

questions.prompt: Why does the author describe cleaner fish and oxpeckers in paragraph 4?
questions.correctAnswer: To provide examples of mutualistic relationships in animals analogous to plant mutualisms

options: To provide examples of mutualistic relationships in animals analogous to plant mutualisms
To show that birds are more intelligent than fish
To explain why mammals have poor immune systems
To argue that all fish are parasitic

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a type of mutualistic interaction?
questions.correctAnswer: Plants competing for sunlight
questions.explanation: The passage discusses cleaner fish, oxpeckers, and parasitic relationships, but not plant competition.
options: Oxpeckers feeding on parasites
Plants competing for sunlight
Obligate and facultative symbioses
Cleaner fish removing parasites

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, approximately what is the annual value of pollination services?

options: Millions of dollars
Tens of billions of dollars

Trillions of dollars

questions.prompt: The word 'pervasive' in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: widespread and present almost everywhere
questions.explanation: 'Pervasive' means existing or spreading throughout, in all places.
options: causing significant damage
recent in development
limited to specific regions
widespread and present almost everywhere

questions.prompt: Which best expresses: 'The evolution of mutualism often involves the development of specialised signalling mechanisms and behavioural adaptations that enable reliable partner recognition and prevent exploitation by cheaters.'
questions.correctAnswer: Mutualistic partners have evolved specific signals and behaviours to identify each other and avoid being exploited
questions.explanation: The sentence conveys how evolutionary pressures shaped communication and behavior in mutualistic species.
options: Mutualistic partners have evolved specific signals and behaviours to identify each other and avoid being exploited
Evolution cannot shape behavior in symbiotic relationships
Cheating is universal in mutualistic relationships
All mutualistic relationships are easily disrupted

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: The main ideas are: mutualism's widespread occurrence (A), specific plant-fungal and plant-pollinator examples (C), and ecological importance (E).
options: A. Mutualism is a widespread and ecologically important form of symbiosis where both organisms benefit from their interaction.
B. Mutualistic relationships are rare and limited to tropical environments.
C. Flowering plant-pollinator and plant-mycorrhizal fungal relationships exemplify ancient, evolved partnerships fundamental to ecosystem structure.
D. All symbiotic relationships are parasitic in nature.
E. Mutualistic relationships provide essential ecosystem services, and their disruption threatens ecosystem stability and human wellbeing.
F. Cleaner fish have no ecological significance in aquatic systems.

questions.prompt: Why does the author contrast the traditional view with modern understanding in paragraph 2?

options: To show how contemporary neuroimaging has revealed that language processing is more distributed than previously thought
To demonstrate that brain imaging cannot provide useful information
To suggest that Broca and Wernicke were wrong about everything
To argue that older theories are always correct

questions.correctAnswer: Different aspects of language (sounds, grammar, meaning) are processed by specialised but interconnected neural systems

options: Language comprehension is a simple, unitary process
Different aspects of language (sounds, grammar, meaning) are processed by specialised but interconnected neural systems
Only one region is involved in language processing
Neural organisation of language is random and unpatterned

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, which of the following is NOT mentioned as evidence of neural plasticity in language learning?
questions.correctAnswer: Children born deaf cannot acquire sign language
questions.explanation: The passage discusses phonological strengthening, second-language learning strategies, and neural reorganisation, but not deaf individuals.
options: Second-language learners recruit different networks initially
Learners shift toward native-speaker neural patterns with practice
Children born deaf cannot acquire sign language
Children strengthen neural pathways for phonological distinctions

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, what symptom characterises Wernicke's aphasia?
questions.correctAnswer: Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states Wernicke's aphasia 'produces fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.'
options: Inability to understand written language
Loss of all speech ability
Preserved comprehension with grammatically poor speech
Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension

questions.prompt: The word 'substrate' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: underlying physical basis or foundation
questions.explanation: 'Neural substrates' refers to the underlying neural structures that support a function.
options: underlying physical basis or foundation
chemical reaction
temporary condition
abstract concept

questions.prompt: Which best expresses: 'Neuroplasticity research suggests that intensive training can partially recover lost language functions by strengthening alternative neural pathways, offering hope for language recovery following brain injury.'
questions.correctAnswer: Intensive practice can help restore some language abilities after brain injury by using alternative neural pathways
questions.explanation: The sentence conveys how neural adaptation enables partial recovery of language following injury.
options: Brain injuries permanently eliminate all language ability
Intensive practice can help restore some language abilities after brain injury by using alternative neural pathways
Language recovery is impossible after any brain damage
Alternative pathways are not involved in language recovery

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,F
questions.explanation: The main ideas are: language involves distributed neural networks (A), modern neuroimaging revealed more complex organization (C), and neuroplasticity enables recovery and learning (F).
options: A. Language involves complex distributed neural networks spanning multiple brain regions rather than being localised to single areas.
B. Only Broca's and Wernicke's areas are involved in language processing.
C. Contemporary neuroimaging has shown that traditional two-area models of language are oversimplified, revealing phonological, syntactic, and semantic processing in distinct regions.
D. Second-language learners never achieve native-like neural patterns.
E. Language disorders are untreatable and always result in permanent disability.
F. Neural plasticity enables both language acquisition in learners and partial recovery of language functions following brain injury through intensive training.
